overview.text: Nowruz (also called Noruz or Persian/Iranian New Year) is a spring festival and new-year observance held at the vernal equinox, traditionally linked with Iranian culture and celebrated in varied forms across many communities. Its name means “new day.” Records connect it to Zoroastrian religious and secular traditions, but its beginnings are not fully certain: the name is absent from surviving Avestan texts, and later stories credit mythical king Jamshid with founding it. The festival matters as a celebration of seasonal renewal and family and community ties. Iranian celebrations may include spring cleaning, visits, and a haft-sin table of symbolic items; in the Bahá’í Faith, Naw-Rúz is a holy day marking the end of the 19-day fast. It is not exclusively a religious holiday; traditions vary by place and faith.

key_facts.text: The name Nowruz means “New Day.” The festival’s exact early history is uncertain: its name does not appear in surviving Old or Young Avestan texts, and it is first attested in Pahlavi texts.
Stories credit Jamshid, a legendary Iranian king, with establishing Nowruz; these are origin legends, not verified historical accounts.
In many Iranian celebrations, families clean their homes, visit one another, and gather around a haft-sin table arranged with symbolic foods and objects.
In the Bahá’í calendar, Naw-Rúz is the first day of the new year and a feast following the 19-day fast; its date is tied to the spring equinox.
Nowruz is recognized by UNESCO as shared intangible cultural heritage, and the United Nations recognizes March 21 as International Nowruz Day.
